claim: Understanding how the brain encodes behaviour is the ultimate goal of neuroscience.
source: Understanding how the brain encodes behaviour is the ultimate goal of neuroscience and the ability to objectively and reproducibly describe and quantify behaviour is a necessary milestone on this path.
evidence: This is a statement about the goals of neuroscience as a field, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: The ability to objectively and reproducibly describe and quantify behaviour is a necessary milestone for understanding how the brain encodes behaviour.
source: Understanding how the brain encodes behaviour is the ultimate goal of neuroscience and the ability to objectively and reproducibly describe and quantify behaviour is a necessary milestone on this path.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for neuroscience research, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Recent technological progresses in machine learning and computational power have boosted the development and adoption of systems leveraging high-resolution video recording to track animal pose and describe behaviour in all four dimensions.
source: Recent technological progresses in machine learning and computational power have boosted the development and adoption of systems leveraging on high-resolution video recording to track an animal pose and describe behaviour in all four dimensions.
evidence: This is a general statement about recent technological developments in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: High temporal and spatial resolution in behavioral tracking systems must come as a compromise with their throughput and accessibility.
source: However, the high temporal and spatial resolution that these systems offer must come as a compromise with their throughput and accessibility.
evidence: This is a statement about the trade-offs in behavioral tracking systems, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Coccinella is an open-source reductionist framework combining high-throughput analysis of behaviour using real-time tracking on a distributed mesh of microcomputers (ethoscopes) with resource-lean statistical learning (HCTSA/Catch22).
source: Here, we describe coccinella, an open-source reductionist framework combining high-throughput analysis of behaviour using real-time tracking on a distributed mesh of microcomputers (ethoscopes) with resource-lean statistical learning (HCTSA/Catch22).
evidence: This is a direct description of the system developed in this study.

claim: Coccinella outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives when exploring the pharmacobehaviour in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Coccinella is a reductionist system, yet outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives when exploring the pharmacobehaviour in Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental comparisons presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 2.

claim: The nervous system integrates stimuli, internal states, expectations, and previous experience to regulate behavioural output.
source: The nervous system integrates stimuli, internal states, expectations, and previous experience to regulate behavioural output.
evidence: This is a statement about nervous system function representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Describing, quantifying, and modulating behaviour are critical aspects of modern neuroscience.
source: Describing, quantifying, and modulating behaviour are critical aspects of modern neuroscience and, ever since its inception, the field has spent considerable effort into building and sharing paradigms or tools aimed at objectively and reproducibly quantify behaviours in the most disparate animal models, to the point that this exercise is now recognised as an exciting subfield of neuroscience in its own right: ethomics (Brown and de Bivort, 2018; Datta et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brown and de Bivort, 2018 and Datta et al., 2019.

claim: Ethomics is now recognised as an exciting subfield of neuroscience in its own right.
source: Describing, quantifying, and modulating behaviour are critical aspects of modern neuroscience and, ever since its inception, the field has spent considerable effort into building and sharing paradigms or tools aimed at objectively and reproducibly quantify behaviours in the most disparate animal models, to the point that this exercise is now recognised as an exciting subfield of neuroscience in its own right: ethomics (Brown and de Bivort, 2018; Datta et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brown and de Bivort, 2018 and Datta et al., 2019.

claim: Ethomics involves collecting data simultaneously from a large number of individuals in a high-throughput fashion.
source: As the portmanteau name itself suggests, ethomics is not just about describing behaviour (etho-) but also about doing so in a high-throughput fashion (-omics), collecting data simultaneously from a large number of individuals, which can remain undisturbed throughout recording.
evidence: This is a definition of ethomics based on the etymology of the term.

claim: The first compromise a researcher faces when choosing a tool for behavioural quantification is between throughput and resolution.
source: Irrespective of the behaviour or the animal model to be analysed, the first compromise a researcher will face when choosing a tool for behavioural quantification will always be between throughput and resolution: a high-throughput analysis will allow for powerful experimental manipulations – such as genetics or pharmacological screens – offering unbiased approaches in identifying neuronal circuits, genes, molecules underpinning behaviour; high-resolution analysis, on the other hand, promises to identify and discriminate even minuscule differences that may not be immediately visible to the human eye, and to label behaviours into identifiable classes (e.g. 'grooming', 'courting', and 'shaking') that may be more relevant to researchers interested in modelling disease or in anthropomorphic descriptions.
evidence: This is a statement about the trade-offs in behavioral analysis tools, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: High-throughput analysis allows for powerful experimental manipulations such as genetics or pharmacological screens.
source: a high-throughput analysis will allow for powerful experimental manipulations – such as genetics or pharmacological screens – offering unbiased approaches in identifying neuronal circuits, genes, molecules underpinning behaviour
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of high-throughput analysis, representing established knowledge.

claim: High-resolution analysis can identify and discriminate even minuscule differences that may not be immediately visible to the human eye.
source: high-resolution analysis, on the other hand, promises to identify and discriminate even minuscule differences that may not be immediately visible to the human eye, and to label behaviours into identifiable classes (e.g. 'grooming', 'courting', and 'shaking') that may be more relevant to researchers interested in modelling disease or in anthropomorphic descriptions.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of high-resolution analysis, representing established knowledge.

claim: The field has generally converged towards the adoption of high-resolution video recording of activity in the past years.
source: In the past years, the field has generally converged towards the adoption of high-resolution video recording of activity, in some cases adopting cameras that have milliseconds temporal resolution or developing setups that provide depth information for three-dimensional reconstruction of motion or posture (Wiltschko et al., 2015; Hsu and Yttri, 2021; Nath et al., 2019; Pereira et al., 2019; Gosztolai et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent work in the field.

claim: High-resolution analyses can be at least in part compatible with high-throughput approaches given recent evolution in machine learning and progresses in computational power.
source: Given the recent evolution in machine learning and progresses in computational power, even these high-resolution analyses can be at least in part compatible with high-throughput approaches (Wiltschko et al., 2020), especially when employed on small invertebrate animal models (McDermott-Rouse et al., 2021; Ayroles et al., 2015; Branson et al., 2009; Kabra et al., 2013) or when aided by robotic handling (Alisch et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent work demonstrating this compatibility.

claim: High-resolution behavioral analysis systems can be prohibitively expensive for most laboratories.
source: These systems, however, can still be prohibitively expensive for most laboratories, and not easily compatible with throughput in the 'omics scale.
evidence: This is a statement about the accessibility of current systems, representing a general observation about the field.

claim: High-resolution behavioral analysis systems are not easily compatible with throughput in the 'omics scale.
source: These systems, however, can still be prohibitively expensive for most laboratories, and not easily compatible with throughput in the 'omics scale.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current systems, representing a general observation about the field.

claim: Coccinella combines high-throughput, inexpensive, real-time ethomics with state-of-the-art statistical analysis.
source: Here, we introduce coccinella: a new experimental framework that combines high-throughput, inexpensive, real-time ethomics (Geissmann et al., 2017) with state-of-the-art statistical analysis (Fulcher and Jones, 2017; Lubba et al., 2019) to characterise and discriminate complex behaviours using a reductionist approach based solely on one simple feature (https://lab.gilest.ro/coccinella).
evidence: This is a description of the system developed in this study, with citations to the underlying technologies.

claim: Coccinella uses a reductionist approach based solely on one simple feature.
source: Here, we introduce coccinella: a new experimental framework that combines high-throughput, inexpensive, real-time ethomics (Geissmann et al., 2017) with state-of-the-art statistical analysis (Fulcher and Jones, 2017; Lubba et al., 2019) to characterise and discriminate complex behaviours using a reductionist approach based solely on one simple feature (https://lab.gilest.ro/coccinella).
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach of the system.

claim: Coccinella builds on ethoscopes, an accessible open-source platform.
source: Coccinella builds on ethoscopes (Geissmann et al., 2017), an accessible open-source platform, to extract, in real-time, activity information from flies.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Geissmann et al., 2017.

claim: Coccinella provides better discernibility at a fraction of the cost compared to state-of-the-art alternatives in recognising the pharmacobehavioural space.
source: Despite its minimalist nature, coccinella outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in recognising the pharmacobehavioural space, providing better discernibility at a fraction of the cost, thus opening a new path to high-throughput ethomics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila ethomics studies generally rely on image acquisition through industrial cameras.
source: Drosophila ethomics studies generally rely on image acquisition through so-called industrial cameras, able to collect videos with high temporal and spatial resolution and featuring mounts for a large selection of lenses.
evidence: This is a statement about common practices in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: Industrial cameras used for Drosophila ethomics are able to collect videos with high temporal and spatial resolution.
source: Drosophila ethomics studies generally rely on image acquisition through so-called industrial cameras, able to collect videos with high temporal and spatial resolution and featuring mounts for a large selection of lenses.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of industrial cameras, representing established knowledge.

claim: Cameras commonly used for Drosophila ethomics (e.g. FLIR, Point Grey, Basler) are expensive.
source: Some of the cameras commonly used for these purposes (e.g. FLIR, Point Grey, Basler) (Mathis et al., 2018) are expensive and normally employed in close-up imaging that microscopically highlights the smallest anatomical features of the animal but at the same time greatly limits the number of experimental subjects that can be recorded by a single device.
evidence: This is a statement about the cost of commonly used cameras, with a citation to Mathis et al., 2018.

claim: Close-up imaging with industrial cameras greatly limits the number of experimental subjects that can be recorded by a single device.
source: Some of the cameras commonly used for these purposes (e.g. FLIR, Point Grey, Basler) (Mathis et al., 2018) are expensive and normally employed in close-up imaging that microscopically highlights the smallest anatomical features of the animal but at the same time greatly limits the number of experimental subjects that can be recorded by a single device.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of close-up imaging, representing established knowledge.

claim: The cost and physical footprint of traditional ethomics setups makes them incompatible with high-throughput simultaneous acquisition for most laboratories.
source: The cost and physical footprint of these setups makes them incompatible, at least for most laboratories, with high-throughput simultaneous acquisition.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of traditional setups, representing a general observation.

claim: Ethoscopes are open source and can be manufactured by a skilled end-user at a cost of about £75 per machine.
source: Ethoscopes are open source and can be manufactured by a skilled end-user at a cost of about £75 per machine, mostly building on two off-the-shelf component: a Raspberry Pi microcomputer and a Raspberry Pi NoIR camera overlooking a bespoke 3D-printed arena hosting freely moving flies.
evidence: This is a statement about the cost and accessibility of ethoscopes.

claim: Ethoscopes are mostly built on two off-the-shelf components: a Raspberry Pi microcomputer and a Raspberry Pi NoIR camera.
source: Ethoscopes are open source and can be manufactured by a skilled end-user at a cost of about £75 per machine, mostly building on two off-the-shelf component: a Raspberry Pi microcomputer and a Raspberry Pi NoIR camera overlooking a bespoke 3D-printed arena hosting freely moving flies.
evidence: This is a description of the hardware components of ethoscopes.

claim: When operating in offline mode, ethoscopes are capable to acquire 720p videos at 60 fps.
source: When operating in offline mode, ethoscopes are capable to acquire 720p videos at 60 fps, which is a convenient option with fast moving animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of ethoscopes in offline mode.

claim: In the default ethoscope working settings, images are analysed by each Raspberry Pi at the very moment they are acquired.
source: In this study, we instead opted for the default ethoscope working settings, providing online tracking and real-time parametric extraction, meaning that images are analysed by each Raspberry Pi at the very moment they are acquired (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the default working mode of ethoscopes used in this study.

claim: The default ethoscope working modality limits the temporal resolution of information being processed to one frame every 444 ± 127 ms, equivalent to 2.2 fps on a Raspberry Pi3.
source: This latter modality limits the temporal resolution of information being processed (one frame every 444 ± 127 ms, equivalent to 2.2 fps on a Raspberry Pi3 at a resolution of 1280 × 960 pixels with each animal being constricted in an ellipse measuring 25.8 ± 1.4 × 9.85 ± 1.4 pixels – Figure 1a) but provides the most affordable and high-throughput solution, dispensing the researcher from organising video storage or asynchronous video processing for tracking the animals.
evidence: This is a measurement of the temporal resolution achieved in this study.

claim: The default ethoscope working modality provides the most affordable and high-throughput solution.
source: This latter modality limits the temporal resolution of information being processed (one frame every 444 ± 127 ms, equivalent to 2.2 fps on a Raspberry Pi3 at a resolution of 1280 × 960 pixels with each animal being constricted in an ellipse measuring 25.8 ± 1.4 × 9.85 ± 1.4 pixels – Figure 1a) but provides the most affordable and high-throughput solution, dispensing the researcher from organising video storage or asynchronous video processing for tracking the animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the default ethoscope working mode.

claim: Flies moved freely in a circular two-dimensional space with a diameter of 11.5 mm.
source: In the work here described, flies moved freely in a circular two-dimensional space with a diameter of 11.5 mm designed to maintain the animal in the walking position (Simon and Dickinson, 2010) while venturing on solidified agar providing nutrients alone or nutrients and drugs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup used in this study.

claim: The circular arena was designed to maintain the animal in the walking position.
source: In the work here described, flies moved freely in a circular two-dimensional space with a diameter of 11.5 mm designed to maintain the animal in the walking position (Simon and Dickinson, 2010) while venturing on solidified agar providing nutrients alone or nutrients and drugs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Simon and Dickinson, 2010.

claim: The maximal velocity of the fly over a period of 10 s best described the basic motion features of the animal in previous analysis of activity and sleep.
source: In previous analysis of activity and sleep (Geissmann et al., 2017; Geissmann, 2018), we found that the maximal velocity of the fly over a period of 10 s best described the basic motion features of the animal, allowing us to accurately differentiate between different activity patterns, such as walking, grooming, and feeding (Geissmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work by Geissmann et al., 2017 and Geissmann, 2018.

claim: Maximal velocity over 10 s allows accurate differentiation between different activity patterns, such as walking, grooming, and feeding.
source: In previous analysis of activity and sleep (Geissmann et al., 2017; Geissmann, 2018), we found that the maximal velocity of the fly over a period of 10 s best described the basic motion features of the animal, allowing us to accurately differentiate between different activity patterns, such as walking, grooming, and feeding (Geissmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Geissmann et al., 2017.

claim: HCTSA is a computational framework that subjects time series to more than 7700 literature-relevant statistical tests.
source: We therefore adopted this measure for coccinella too, ultimately producing monodimensional time series of a behavioural correlate, which were then digested using highly comparative time-series analysis (HCTSA) (Fulcher and Jones, 2017), a computational framework that effortlessly subjects time series to more than 7700 literature-relevant statistical tests, looking for meaningful discriminative features.
evidence: This is a description of HCTSA with a citation to Fulcher and Jones, 2017.

claim: Features extracted through HCTSA were used to classify behaviour using a linear support vector machine (SVMlinear).
source: Features successfully extracted through HCTSA were then used to classify behaviour using a linear support vector machine (SVMlinear) (Chatterjee et al., 2022; Figure 1b) and here presented and compared using confusion matrices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the classification method used in this study, with a citation to Chatterjee et al., 2022.

claim: The system was tested by exploring the pharmacobehavioural space of flies fed with a panel of known or putative neurotropic chemicals.
source: To test the ability of this system to discriminate behaviour, we started by exploring the pharmacobehavioural space of flies fed with a panel of known or putative neurotropic chemicals, comprising molecules previously described in the literature along with uncharacterised ones being considered as potential insecticides (Figure 1c, d and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used to test the system.

claim: Using an initial panel of 17 treatments (16 drugs and 1 solvent control), the system was able to discern compounds with an accuracy of 71.4%.
source: Using an initial panel of 17 treatments (16 drugs and 1 solvent control) we were able to discern compounds with an accuracy of 71.4% (vs. 5.8% of a random classifier – Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: A random classifier would have an accuracy of 5.8% for 17 treatments.
source: Using an initial panel of 17 treatments (16 drugs and 1 solvent control) we were able to discern compounds with an accuracy of 71.4% (vs. 5.8% of a random classifier – Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a calculated baseline for comparison with the experimental results.

claim: Dieldrin was predicted with an accuracy of 94%.
source: Some compounds induced behaviours with a particularly high predictive fingerprint: dieldrin, for instance, was predicted with an accuracy of 94% and flonicamid with an accuracy of 87%.
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data.

claim: Flonicamid was predicted with an accuracy of 87%.
source: Some compounds induced behaviours with a particularly high predictive fingerprint: dieldrin, for instance, was predicted with an accuracy of 94% and flonicamid with an accuracy of 87%.
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data.

claim: Tetramethrin showed 41% accuracy.
source: For others, our system fared more poorly (e.g. tetramethrin showed 41% accuracy).
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data.

claim: All compounds were correctly identified as the first choice with the first predicted compounds having, on average, a score that was 15 times greater compared to the second-best choices.
source: In all cases, however, the relative confusion was negligible, with all compounds being correctly identified as the first choice and with the first predicted compounds having, on average, a score that was 15 times greater compared to the second-best choices (Figure 1c – min.: 3.3×; max.: 65×).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: The minimum ratio between first and second-best choices was 3.3×.
source: In all cases, however, the relative confusion was negligible, with all compounds being correctly identified as the first choice and with the first predicted compounds having, on average, a score that was 15 times greater compared to the second-best choices (Figure 1c – min.: 3.3×; max.: 65×).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The maximum ratio between first and second-best choices was 65×.
source: In all cases, however, the relative confusion was negligible, with all compounds being correctly identified as the first choice and with the first predicted compounds having, on average, a score that was 15 times greater compared to the second-best choices (Figure 1c – min.: 3.3×; max.: 65×).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Feeding flies with different concentrations of drugs showed a different effect on short-term lethality.
source: Feeding flies with different concentrations of drugs unsurprisingly showed a different effect on short-term lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), with several compounds hitting a 25% lethality rate before the end of the experiment when fed at the highest concentration (1000 ppm – Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Several compounds hit a 25% lethality rate before the end of the experiment when fed at the highest concentration (1000 ppm).
source: Feeding flies with different concentrations of drugs unsurprisingly showed a different effect on short-term lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), with several compounds hitting a 25% lethality rate before the end of the experiment when fed at the highest concentration (1000 ppm – Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Lowering the compound concentration, the predictive accuracy of the system decreased from 71.4% (1000 ppm) to 61.8% (100 ppm), falling to 36.1% with the lowest concentrations (1 ppm).
source: Lowering the compound concentration, the predictive accuracy of the system decreased from 71.4% (1000 ppm) to 61.8% (100 ppm), falling to 36.1% with the lowest concentrations (1 ppm), indicating that the system does operate on pharmacologically induced, biologically meaningful behavioural correlates (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: The decrease in accuracy with lower compound concentrations indicates that the system operates on pharmacologically induced, biologically meaningful behavioural correlates.
source: Lowering the compound concentration, the predictive accuracy of the system decreased from 71.4% (1000 ppm) to 61.8% (100 ppm), falling to 36.1% with the lowest concentrations (1 ppm), indicating that the system does operate on pharmacologically induced, biologically meaningful behavioural correlates (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing dose-dependent effects.

claim: The paraL1029F allele encodes for a version of the α-subunit of voltage-gated sodium channel conferring resistance to dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and pyrethroids.
source: the paraL1029F allele encodes for a version of the α-subunit of voltage-gated sodium channel conferring resistance to dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and pyrethroids (Kaduskar et al., 2022)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kaduskar et al., 2022.

claim: The RdlA301S allele encodes for a version of the ligand-gated chloride channel conferring resistance to dieldrin and fiproles.
source: the RdlA301S allele encodes for a version of the ligand-gated chloride channel conferring resistance to dieldrin and fiproles (Remnant et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Remnant et al., 2014.

claim: Challenging genetic mutants with their respective compounds created confusion in the clustering algorithm for discerning between drug treatment and solvent control.
source: Challenging these mutants with their respective compounds created confusion in the clustering algorithm for which discerning between drug treatment and solvent control became a harder task, especially in the case of DDT and paraL1029F (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The observed drop in accuracy with drug-resistant mutants suggests that coccinella is working on biologically relevant behavioural signatures.
source: The observed drop in accuracy suggests again that coccinella is working on biologically relevant behavioural signatures and the fact that some discrimination can still be observed with targets harbouring point mutations – which should severely affect compound efficacy – is indicative of high sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with drug-resistant mutants.

claim: The fact that some discrimination can still be observed with targets harbouring point mutations is indicative of high sensitivity.
source: The observed drop in accuracy suggests again that coccinella is working on biologically relevant behavioural signatures and the fact that some discrimination can still be observed with targets harbouring point mutations – which should severely affect compound efficacy – is indicative of high sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with drug-resistant mutants.

claim: A total of 2192 flies were subjected to a panel of 40 treatments.
source: Having established the accuracy and sensitivity of the system, we next wanted to test its usefulness in a genuine high-throughput scenario. We subjected a total of 2192 flies to a panel of 40 treatments (Figure 1d), mostly featuring known compounds but also two unexplored molecules (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for the high-throughput test.

claim: The 100 ppm intermediate concentrations showed the best compromise between accuracy and lethality in the pilot experiment.
source: Given that the 100 ppm intermediate concentrations showed the best compromise between accuracy and lethality in the previous pilot experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), we performed this larger screen using compounds diluted at 100 ppm only.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pilot experiment data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: With a panel of 40 treatments, the system was able to first-guess 39 out of 40 of the tested treatments.
source: Even with such a large panel, the system was able to first-guess 39 out of 40 of the tested treatments (the only exception being the Syngenta Compound #5) with an overall accuracy of 44.5% vs. 2.5% of the random classifier.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The only exception to first-guess accuracy in the 40-treatment panel was Syngenta Compound #5.
source: Even with such a large panel, the system was able to first-guess 39 out of 40 of the tested treatments (the only exception being the Syngenta Compound #5) with an overall accuracy of 44.5% vs. 2.5% of the random classifier.
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data.

claim: With 40 treatments, the overall accuracy was 44.5% vs. 2.5% of the random classifier.
source: Even with such a large panel, the system was able to first-guess 39 out of 40 of the tested treatments (the only exception being the Syngenta Compound #5) with an overall accuracy of 44.5% vs. 2.5% of the random classifier.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Parallel experiments were run in which flies were fed with a selected panel of 12 treatments (11 drugs and a solvent control) and their behaviour analysed using coccinella or other widely adopted state-of-the-art methods.
source: To quantify any possible loss in information content, we ran a series of parallel experiments in which flies were fed with a selected panel of 12 treatments (11 drugs and a solvent control, Figure 2) and their behaviour analysed either using coccinella or using other widely adopted state-of-the-art methods, which started with high-resolution imaging and employed supervised machine learning for pose-estimation DeepLabCut; Mathis et al., 2018 followed by unsupervised identification of behavioural grammar (B-SOiD; Hsu and Yttri, 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the comparative experimental design.

claim: State-of-the-art methods used for comparison started with high-resolution imaging and employed supervised machine learning for pose-estimation (DeepLabCut) followed by unsupervised identification of behavioural grammar (B-SOiD).
source: To quantify any possible loss in information content, we ran a series of parallel experiments in which flies were fed with a selected panel of 12 treatments (11 drugs and a solvent control, Figure 2) and their behaviour analysed either using coccinella or using other widely adopted state-of-the-art methods, which started with high-resolution imaging and employed supervised machine learning for pose-estimation DeepLabCut; Mathis et al., 2018 followed by unsupervised identification of behavioural grammar (B-SOiD; Hsu and Yttri, 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the comparison methods with citations to Mathis et al., 2018 and Hsu and Yttri, 2021.

claim: Data were either immediately clustered using different common clustering algorithms (K-nearest neighbours, random forest) or first processed through Catch22 before being clustered using SVMlinear.
source: To widen the range of comparisons, data were then either immediately clustered using different common clustering algorithms (K-nearest neighbours, random forest) or first processed through a smaller, selected subsample of the HCTSA array (Catch22; Lubba et al., 2019) before being clustered using SVMlinear (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a description of the different analytical approaches used for comparison, with a citation to Lubba et al., 2019.

claim: In the comparison challenge, coccinella unambiguously identified 10 out of 12 compounds with an overall accuracy of 42.4% vs. 8.3% of the random classifier.
source: In this challenge, coccinella unambiguously identified 10 out of 12 compounds, with poor performance only for two of them (flubendiamide and tetramethrin) and an overall accuracy of 42.4% vs. 8.3% of the random classifier (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative experimental data presented in Figure 2b.

claim: Coccinella showed poor performance only for flubendiamide and tetramethrin in the 12-compound comparison.
source: In this challenge, coccinella unambiguously identified 10 out of 12 compounds, with poor performance only for two of them (flubendiamide and tetramethrin) and an overall accuracy of 42.4% vs. 8.3% of the random classifier (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a specific result from the comparative experimental data.

claim: None of the state-of-the-art high-resolution paths did better than coccinella in the comparison challenge.
source: Surprisingly, none of the state-of-the-art high-resolution paths did better than this.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the results of different methods.

claim: The combination of pose-estimation → grammar extraction → random forest classification scored as the second best, with an accuracy of 25.4% but with only three compounds being unambiguously identified.
source: The combination of pose-estimation → grammar extraction → random forest classification scored as the second best, with an accuracy of 25.4% but with only three compounds being unambiguously identified (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative experimental data presented in Figure 2c.

claim: The same experimental dataset clustered with poorer performance when using K-nearest neighbours.
source: The same experimental dataset clustered with even poorer performance when using K-nearest neighbours (Figure 2e) and even the application of HCTSA features extraction to the B-SoID output still could not match the accuracy observed with coccinella's reductionist approach (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative experimental data presented in Figure 2e.

claim: The application of HCTSA features extraction to the B-SoID output still could not match the accuracy observed with coccinella's reductionist approach.
source: The same experimental dataset clustered with even poorer performance when using K-nearest neighbours (Figure 2e) and even the application of HCTSA features extraction to the B-SoID output still could not match the accuracy observed with coccinella's reductionist approach (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative experimental data presented in Figure 2d.

claim: Some alternative combination of state-of-the-art approaches will probably manage to match or likely improve over coccinella's performance.
source: This analysis is not meant to be conclusive. We expect that some alternative combination of state-of-the-art approaches will probably manage to match or likely improve over coccinella's performance, yet the fact we could obtain such an impressive result with a system that is arguably unmatched in terms of throughput and economic cost is, alone, an argument that gives new weight to this (and future) reductionist approaches.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future possibilities.

claim: The impressive result obtained with coccinella, which is unmatched in terms of throughput and economic cost, gives new weight to reductionist approaches.
source: This analysis is not meant to be conclusive. We expect that some alternative combination of state-of-the-art approaches will probably manage to match or likely improve over coccinella's performance, yet the fact we could obtain such an impressive result with a system that is arguably unmatched in terms of throughput and economic cost is, alone, an argument that gives new weight to this (and future) reductionist approaches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative experimental results.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster shows a strong, conserved homeostatic regulation of sleep that forces flies to recover at least in part lost sleep after forceful sleep deprivation.
source: Drosophila melanogaster is known to show a strong, conserved homeostatic regulation of sleep that forces flies to recover at least in part lost sleep, for instance after a night of forceful sleep deprivation (Shaw et al., 2000; Hendricks et al., 2000).
